a: the stumbling blocks together with the wicked
t: Stumbling blocks, or the wicked who stumble?
p: The Greek has "the wicked will stumble" where the Hebrew has "the stumbling blocks with the wicked."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and the stumbling blocks with the wicked
readings.plain: the stumbling blocks together with the wicked

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and the ungodly will grow weak

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading and has a plain sense (idols or ruins are swept away with the wicked). The Greek smooths a rare noun into a verb. The word is found only here and in Isaiah 3:6.
b: The Dead Sea scroll 4QXII-b (4Q77) is preserved at 1:2 and its transcription has no words for 1:3, so it gives no help. Mur88 begins at 1:1 and then 1:11.

t: Humankind or the lawless?
p: The Greek says "I will remove the lawless" where the Hebrew says "I will cut off humankind."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and I will cut off humankind (the human)

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and I will remove the lawless
readings.plain: I will cut off the lawless

why: The Hebrew repeats "humankind" from the list in the verse and plays on 'adam and 'adamah. The Greek brings the sentence into line with the earlier "the ungodly" and makes the judgment moral rather than total. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The Greek translator softens the sweep of 1:2-3: in the Greek, only the lawless are removed from the earth.

t: A remnant of Baal or the names of Baal?
p: The Greek reads "the names of Baal" where the Hebrew has "the remnant of Baal."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: the remnant of the Baal

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: the names of Baal (the Greek uses a feminine article)

why: "Remnant" (she'ar) is the harder reading; "names" may come from the next phrase, "the name of the idol priests," or from a Hebrew text with shem. The remnant of Baal suits a time of reform, when some of the old cult was already gone.
b: The Greek translators write the feminine article before Baal throughout the prophets, a habit usually explained by the Hebrew word "shame" (bosheth), which readers spoke in place of Baal. The scrolls do not preserve this verse.

t: Milcom, or "their king"?
p: The same Hebrew letters can be read as the god Milcom or as "their king."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (the Hebrew letters can also be read malkam); Jerome's Latin Vulgate (Melchom)
readings.en: by Malcam (Milcom)

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: by their king

why: The letters are the same; only the vowel marks differ. The Ammonite god is called Milcom in 1 Kings 11:5, 33; 2 Kings 23:13 and Malcam in Jeremiah 49:1, 3, and Zephaniah is paired with Josiah's reform of the shrines built for him. The Greek "their king" may mean the LORD, a human king or the god; the Hebrew context, swearing by a god, favors Milcom.
b: Milcom was the god of Ammon, worshiped at a shrine Solomon built (1 Kings 11:5, 7) that Josiah defiled (2 Kings 23:13). Swearing by him beside the LORD is the syncretism of the verse.

t: Their masters' house, or the house of the LORD their God?
p: The Greek has "the house of the LORD their God"; the Hebrew has "the house of their masters."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: the house of their masters (lords)

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: the house of the LORD their God
readings.plain: the house of the LORD their God

why: "Masters" is the harder reading and could be the king, the officials or their gods. The Greek spells out the Temple, which would make the sin temple violence, but then the verse would not need the "leaping" over the doorsill. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The Greek also reads "openly" and "porches" where the Hebrew has "doorsill," and "impiety" for "violence."

t: The Fish Gate, or the gate of the piercers?
p: The Greek reads "the gate of those who pierce" where the Hebrew has "the Fish Gate."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: from the Fish Gate

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: from the gate of those who pierce

why: The Fish Gate is a known gate of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 33:14; Nehemiah 3:3). The Greek may have read a different word (daqar, "pierce") or tried to make sense of an unfamiliar name.
b: The Greek also reads "from the second" for "the Second District."

t: Bodies, flesh or guts?
p: The Hebrew word is rare; the Greek reads "flesh," the Latin "bodies"; some translations read "entrails."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and their ... like dung (lechumam)

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ τὰς σάρκας αὐτῶν ὡς βόλβιτα
readings.en: and their flesh like dung

why: The Hebrew word looks like "bread" (lechem) with a suffix, but the context needs a part of the body: perhaps "flesh" (compare Arabic lahm) or "guts." The Plain English Translation uses the wider "bodies."
b: Mur88 has this line, but the transcription shows this word as restored by the editors, so the scroll gives no evidence here.

t: Without shame, not longed for, or untaught?
p: The Hebrew word nikhsaf can be read three ways, and the Greek goes a fourth.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 agrees (the word is preserved)
readings.en: a nation not ashamed / not pale with shame

readings.w: King James Version and Young's Literal Translation take the same Hebrew word as "longed for" (kasaf, as in Psalm 84:2)
readings.en: a nation not desired

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: the untaught (undisciplined) nation

why: A related Aramaic and later Hebrew sense of the root is "grow pale, be ashamed," and the context (a call to gather and examine oneself) favors "shameless," which is how most modern translations read it. "Not longed for" is possible, "not desired" or "unwanted," and gives a sad edge (Genesis 31:30 and Psalm 84:2 use the root for longing).
b: The scroll Mur88 reads the verse with the same Hebrew letters.

t: A decree being born, or a flower passing by?
p: The Greek reads "before you become like a passing flower" where the Hebrew has "before the decree gives birth."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 agrees (the word before "decree" is preserved)
readings.en: before the decree is born (brings forth)

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι ὑμᾶς ὡς ἄνθος παραπορευόμενον
readings.en: before you become like a blossom passing by
readings.plain: before you become like a passing flower

why: The Hebrew line is hard, which marks it as the original: the decree is spoken of as a pregnancy that ends in the day of the LORD. The Greek reads the Hebrew verb for "give birth" and the noun for "chaff" as "become... like a flower" and drops "decree."
b: The line continues with "the day passes like chaff." The Greek has no word for chaff.

t: Dug wells, or Crete?
p: The Hebrew word kerot (digging, wells?) is read "Crete" in the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: digging(s), wells

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: Crete a pasture of flocks

why: The Greek read the Hebrew letters k-r-t as Crete, in agreement with the Kerethites of verse 5. The Hebrew word is uncertain, but "digging, dug places, wells" makes sense with shepherds and flocks. The scroll Mur88 has these letters but they are restored by the editors.
b: This verse is the main reason for the Greek reading in 2:5 "neighbors of the Cretans."

t: Their fortunes, or their captivity?
p: The Hebrew text has two spellings of the noun, shevut and shevit, and the Greek translates "captivity."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (the Leningrad Codex writes shevitam; other Masoretic traditions have shevutam)
readings.en: and he will turn their fortunes (shevut/shevit)

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and he will bring back their captivity

why: The same idiom, shuv shevut, is used in Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3 and Job 42:10, and in Job there is no exile at all, so "fortunes" is the safer meaning. The Plain English Translation follows the site term used in Jeremiah. See Zephaniah 3:20.
b: The two spellings of the noun, shevit and shevut, are recorded in the Hebrew tradition for this phrase here and in 3:20; both are one word in meaning. Mur88 restores the noun (it is in brackets in the transcription), so no scroll spelling is evidence either way.

t: Nettles, or Damascus?
p: Where the Hebrew has "a place of nettles," the Greek has "Damascus."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: a place possessed by nettles

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ Δαμασκὸς ἐκλελιμμένη ὡς θιμωνιὰ ἅλωνος
readings.en: and Damascus left like a heap on a threshing floor
readings.plain: Damascus, left like a pile on a threshing floor

why: The Hebrew word mimshaq looks like Damascus (Dammeseq) in unvoweled script, and the Greek may have read it so. The Hebrew phrase is also good Hebrew (compare Proverbs 24:31). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: Damascus appears nowhere else in Zephaniah; the Greek adds it to the list of those struck.

t: My nation, or the nation?
p: A written/read difference: the Hebrew text is written "the nation" and read "my nation."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (Qere goyi); Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus) ("my nation")
readings.en: my nation

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (Ketiv goy)
readings.en: the nation

why: The word is parallel to "my people" in the previous line, and God is speaking, so "my nation" fits. The Greek agrees. The written form may be an old spelling of "my nation."
b: The Ketiv-Qere system of the Masoretes marks a difference between the written consonants and the reading tradition (see the topic ketiv-qere).

a: animals of every sort, a whole nation of them
t: Animals of a nation, or animals of the earth?
p: The Hebrew says "every animal of a nation"; the Greek says "all the wild animals of the earth."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXII-b (4Q77) agrees (the word goy is preserved there; Mur88 restores it)
readings.en: every beast of a nation
readings.plain: animals of every sort, a whole nation of them

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: all the wild beasts of the earth
readings.plain: all the wild animals of the earth

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading. "Nation" (goy) can mean a swarm of animals, as in Joel 1:6 for locusts. The Greek may have read erets, "earth," or smoothed an odd phrase.
b: 4QXII-b (4Q77) preserves the words "every animal of the nation" in 2:14 as in the Masoretic Text.

t: Wreckage, or ravens?
p: The Greek has "ravens at the gateways" where the Hebrew has "ruin on the doorsill."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXII-b (4Q77) and Mur88 agree
readings.en: devastation (choreb) on the threshold

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: ravens in its gateways

why: The Hebrew consonants for "ruin" (ch-r-b) differ from "raven" ('-r-b) by one letter, and the Greek could be a reading of 'oreb. Both 4Q77 and Mur88 have the consonants of "ruin" here. The line before has birds in the window, which could have prompted the change.
b: The Greek rendering fits the scene of birds in a ruin but the scrolls read "ruin."

a: for he has torn the cedar paneling bare
t: Cedar paneling laid bare, or cedar in its height?
p: The Greek says "for its height is cedar"; the Hebrew says the cedar work is laid bare.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXII-b (4Q77) and Mur88 agree
readings.en: for the cedar work he has laid bare
readings.plain: for he has torn the cedar paneling bare

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: because the cedar is its height (stature)
readings.plain: for its tall building is cedar

why: 'Arzah is a rare form (cedar work); 'erah means "laid bare." Both scrolls have the same words. The Greek takes 'erah as something like "its height" and keeps the cedar as a statement about the building.
b: Jeremiah 22:14-15 shows the cedar paneling of a Judean palace.

t: The oppressing city, or the dove?
p: The Greek and Jerome's Latin read "the dove" where the Hebrew points "the oppressing."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXII-c (4Q78) preserves "the dove" (hayyonah) and restores "the city"; Mur88 preserves "the city, the dove"
readings.en: the city, the oppressing (yonah from yanah)

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus); Jerome's Latin Vulgate (civitas columba)
readings.en: the dove

why: The same letters spell "the dove" (yonah) and, with a different root, "the oppressing." The Hebrew pointing and the next verses (oppression in the city) favor the second; the dove reading may have come from Hosea 7:11 or from the sense that Jerusalem was once the faithful one.
b: The Hebrew Bible uses yonah for oppression in Jeremiah 46:16 and 50:16, "the oppressing sword."

t: Rebellious and defiled, or splendid and redeemed?
p: The same letters can be read "rebellious and defiled" (Hebrew) or "splendid and redeemed" (Greek).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXII-c (4Q78) preserves the first word and Mur88 the second, each restoring the other, so the consonants are covered between them
readings.en: rebellious (or filthy) and defiled

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: the conspicuous (splendid) and redeemed

why: Both words are written with letters that can be read two ways. The first (m-r-') can be "rebel, be filthy" (the KJV has "filthy") or "appearance, splendor." The second (g-'-l) can be "redeem" or "defile" (as in Malachi 1:7). The Hebrew reading fits the "Woe to" at the start. The Greek turns the line into sarcasm or praise.
b: Between them the scrolls preserve the consonants. The question is how to vowel them.

t: Wolves of the evening, or of Arabia?
p: The Hebrew word 'erev means evening; the Greek reads 'arav, Arabia.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXII-g (4Q82) preserves the end of the verse
readings.en: wolves of the evening

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: wolves of Arabia

why: The Hebrew has Habakkuk 1:8 as a parallel ("evening wolves"). The Greek could read the same letters as 'arav; Jeremiah 5:6 has "wolf of the desert plains" ('aravot). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: 4QXII-g (4Q82) has the last words of the verse, "they do not leave anything for the morning," but the word for evening is restored by the editors.

a: Then her home will not be cut off
t: Her home, or from her eyes?
p: The Greek reads "from her eyes" where the Hebrew has "her home."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and her dwelling will not be cut off
readings.plain: Then her home will not be cut off

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ οὐ μὴ ἐξολοθρευθῆτε ἐξ ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῆς
readings.en: and you will not be destroyed from her eyes
readings.plain: Then you will not be cut off from her sight

why: The letters m-'-w-n-h (her dwelling) and m-'-y-n-h (from her eyes) are one letter apart. The Hebrew makes sense of the cutting off of a home, which is the exile threatened throughout the book. The Greek continues differently: "Get ready, rise early, all their gleanings are ruined," where the Hebrew says they rose early and corrupted all their deeds.
b: The scrolls do not preserve the verse (the transcription shows no scroll here).

t: A witness, plunder or "forever"?
p: The Hebrew letters l-'-d can be read three ways, and translations differ.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (eis martyrion, "for a witness")
readings.en: for a witness

readings.w: King James Version ("the prey"); many modern translations ("to seize the prey")
readings.en: for plunder (prey)

readings.w: Jerome's Latin Vulgate (in futurum, "for the future")
readings.en: forever (for the future)

why: The Hebrew with its traditional vowels says the LORD rises up as a witness against the nations, and the Greek agrees. The reading "plunder" repoints the letters and fits the picture of the LORD as a conqueror taking prey. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and the Greek together.
b: Mur88 has this passage, but the word is restored in the transcription, so it gives no evidence here.

a: change the lips of the peoples into pure lips
t: Pure lips, or something else?
p: The Greek has "I will turn upon the peoples a tongue for its generation," which is hard to relate to the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 reads "the peoples" with the article and the same words "pure lip"
readings.en: I will turn to peoples a pure lip
readings.plain: change the lips of the peoples into pure lips

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: μεταστρέψω ἐπὶ λαοὺς γλῶσσαν εἰς γενεὰν αὐτῆς
readings.en: I will turn a tongue on peoples, to its generation
readings.plain: change the language of the peoples, each for its own generation

why: The Hebrew is clear and Mur88 has "pure lip." The Greek could be reading the Hebrew word for "pure" as something like "her generation," but the result is obscure. The Greek ends with "under one yoke" for "one shoulder."
b: See the notes on this verse for the meaning of "lip" and "pure."

a: He has swept your enemy away.
t: One enemy, or enemies?
p: The Greek and the scroll Mur88 appear to read "your enemies," plural.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: he has cleared away your enemy
readings.plain: He has swept your enemy away.

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus); Mur88 (spelled with an added yod that may mean the plural)
readings.en: your enemies
readings.plain: He has swept your enemies away.

why: The singular is used collectively in Hebrew for the enemy force, so the difference is small. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The transcription marks Mur88's word as differing only by a vowel letter; it could be a plural or a fuller spelling.

a: You will not fear harm again.
t: Fear harm, or see harm?
p: The Hebrew has "you will fear"; the Greek has "you will see," and the site's automatic notes record a Hebrew spelling for "see."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: you will not fear evil again
readings.plain: You will not fear harm again.

readings.w: A Hebrew spelling recorded as a variant in the site's automatic notes (tir'i, "you will see," from ra'ah); the source does not name the witness
readings.en: you will not see evil again
readings.plain: You will not see harm again.

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus), which agrees with the "see" spelling
readings.en: you will not see evil again
readings.plain: You will not see harm again.

why: "Fear" is written with a yod (tire'i) and "see" without it (tir'i), and the two sound alike. The Leningrad Codex has "fear". The automatic notes record a Hebrew variant with "see", and the Greek agrees with it, so this is a difference in the Hebrew tradition and not only in the vowel signs. The scroll Mur88 is no help: its word is restored (in brackets in the transcription). The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text because the next verse begins "Do not be afraid," and "fear" fits that. "See harm" is good sense too.
b: Mur88 is damaged at this word, so the scrolls give no evidence on "fear" or "see".

a: He will be quiet in his love.
t: Quiet in his love, or renew you in his love?
p: The Greek says "he will renew you in his love" where the Hebrew says "he will be quiet."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 reads the same word
readings.en: he will be silent (or quiet) in his love
readings.plain: He will be quiet in his love.

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καινιεῖ σε ἐν τῇ ἀγαπήσει αὐτοῦ
readings.en: he will renew you in his love
readings.plain: He will renew you in his love.

why: The Greek would come from a Hebrew yachadesh ("renew"), which differs from yacharish ("be silent") by one letter, resh for dalet, which look alike in many scripts. The Hebrew is the harder reading, and Mur88 preserves it, which shows the Hebrew text of the early 100s AD. Jerome's Latin has silebit, "he will be silent." The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: Four readings of the Hebrew word are possible: "he will be silent" about their sins; "he will be quiet" in the fullness of love; "he will quiet you" (a causative); and, with the Greek, "he will renew you."

a: I will gather those who grieve over the appointed feast
t: A broken verse in Hebrew and Greek
p: The Hebrew is hard and the Greek reads "I will gather the crushed. Woe: who took reproach on her?"

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 agrees on the consonants
readings.orig: נוּגֵי מִמּוֹעֵד אָסַפְתִּי מִמֵּךְ הָיוּ מַשְׂאֵת עָלֶיהָ חֶרְפָּה
readings.en: those grieved from the appointed feast I have gathered; from you they were; a burden on her, reproach
readings.plain: I will gather those who grieve over the appointed feast

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ συνάξω τοὺς συντετριμμένους· οὐαί, τίς ἔλαβεν ἐπ᾽ αὐτὴν ὀνειδισμόν;
readings.en: and I will gather the crushed; woe, who took reproach upon her?

why: The Greek is a very different text. The Hebrew can be translated, though not smoothly, and the Plain English Translation gives its best sense. Mur88 has most of the verse in the same letters as the Masoretic Text, so the difficulty is old.
b: King James Version: "them that are sorrowful for the solemn assembly"; Young's: "mine afflicted from the appointed place." No translation reads the verse without help.
